extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and social scientists interested in scientific method and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for forming and evaluating scientific theories about individual character and social phenomena, emphasizing the proper interplay of deduction and induction and the limitations of experimental/empirical methods in complex social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification a posteriori pari passu with deduction a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification a posteriori must proceed pari passu with deduction a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inferences given by theory must be tested by specific experience whenever obtainable; conclusions of theory cannot be trusted unless confirmed by observation, nor those of observation unless they can be affiliated to theory. The consilience of a priori reasoning and specific experience forms the only sufficient ground for principles in sciences dealing with complex phenomena (e.g., Ethology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain highest generalizations first when induction conditions allow
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever means of investigation can reach causes, the simplest cases (fewest causes) are most amenable to induction and tend to yield the most comprehensive laws; therefore in sciences of causes it is usually desirable to obtain the highest generalizations first and deduce more special ones from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept the caricature that starting from high generalizations is always 'vicious' — it is appropriate when supported by rigorous inductive methods and subsequent verification. Example: laws of motion were early and general and later shown widely applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose ethology as deductive science from psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethology (science of the formation of character) should be a deductive system of corollaries from Psychology (the experimental science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creation of Ethology requires: (1) deducing theoretically the ethological consequences of particular circumstances and comparing them with common experience, and (2) empirical study of human types and circumstances to explain characteristics by psychological laws; any residuals are attributed to congenital predispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of social science: explain causes and guide action, not universal precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the Social Science is to determine causes of social phenomena and to understand what effects features of social states are likely to produce, and how effects might be prevented, modified, or accelerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect universal practical maxims; art must adapt measures to particular cases. Science may ascertain general laws, but the corresponding art often lacks universal precepts because circumstances vary infinitely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes (social phenomena derive from individual human nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: All phenomena of society are phenomena of human nature, generated by the action of outward circumstances upon masses of human beings: human beings in society have no properties but those derived from individual human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social phenomena should therefore be analyzed by resolving them into the laws of individual human actions and passions; treat social effects as composite results of individual causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject naive experimental/chemical method for social science
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chemical (experimental) mode — treating political facts as directly experimental like chemical facts and demanding specific experience in all cases — is inadequate for social science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drawing general conclusions from single unanalyzed instances or historical anecdotes. Experimental demands (controlled variation, ability to repeat and isolate causes) cannot be met in social contexts; practitioners using isolated historical examples as proof are committing a logical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference: requirement and impracticability in social science
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of Difference requires finding two instances identical in all respects except the one under inquiry; this is manifestly impossible for nations/societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legislative and institutional differences are themselves effects of prior causes, there can be no two societies identical in all but one respect; attempting to apply this method in social science yields illusory 'experimentum crucis' results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference: limits when multiple favorable circumstances exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect Method of Difference compares classes of instances that each share a circumstance; even this approach is inconclusive because prosperity (or similar outcomes) is typically the result of many favorable circumstances, which may be distributed among comparison groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A restrictive nation might combine multiple favorable causes split across comparator nations, so failure of comparators to prosper does not demonstrate causation by the one differing policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement: weak in cases of plurality of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of Agreement (finding a common antecedent among instances sharing an effect) raises little presumption of causation if the effect admits multiple causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if several prosperous nations share only one antecedent, the inference that it caused prosperity is trivial when many causes can produce the effect; at best you learn the effect can occur without some antecedents, not that a common antecedent is the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations: unreliable for aggregate social attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of Concomitant Variations (correlating quantitative changes in antecedents and consequences) is undermined in social science because aggregate attributes are influenced by innumerable causes and interdependent elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because different agents' effects are not neatly separable and influence attributes indirectly through mutual action, aggregate variations will not bear uniform proportion to any single component's variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues: useful only when part of causes are known deductively
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of Residues attributes unexplained remainder of an effect, after accounting for known causes, to other known circumstances; applied to social phenomena it presupposes known causes that cannot be established by specific experience alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is not purely empirical; it relies on previously deduced principles of human nature. Thus experimental argument in social science typically serves only to verify conclusions drawn from general laws of human motives and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of elimination, comparison, and careful weighing of historical instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Valid inference from historical or contemporary instances requires careful selection, elimination of confounders, and weighing of points of likeness and difference rather than casual numbering of coincidences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring general rules from casual coincidences or singular historical examples; where Coleridge’s practice compared resemblances, one must weigh which similarities are capable of influencing the effect before attributing residual effects to differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on prediction versus usefulness for guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Although social laws may exist, prediction is limited by the multiplicity and changeability of data (circumstances); nevertheless, knowledge of causes can be valuable for understanding past development, anticipating tendencies, and guiding action in known conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake limited predictive power for lack of scientific character; aim for explanations that clarify causes and probable tendencies in given, well-understood circumstances rather than long-range deterministic forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer deduction from principles of human nature when induction is infeasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where specific experience cannot supply the requisites for valid induction (due to plurality of causes and inability to control variation), resorting to deduction from general laws of human nature is legitimate and often necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental observations are then used as supplementary verification of deductions; insisting on pure empirical proof in such cases misunderstands the nature of social inquiry and may obstruct sound reasoning.
